pinterest.title: Palestinian Wedding Traditions: The Customs, in the Order a Family Lives Them
pinterest.description: A Palestinian wedding is rarely one evening. Celebrations often run over several days, beginning with the tulbeh, the formal asking made by the groom's family, then a sahra evening, a henna night, the zaffeh procession, dabke and a shared feast. Our guide to Palestinian wedding traditions explains what each custom involves and what it asks of a venue, for a wedding at home in Australia or abroad.

pinterest.title: Tatreez and the Palestinian Wedding Dress: What the Embroidery Tells You
pinterest.description: In 2021, UNESCO inscribed the art of embroidery in Palestine on its Representative List. The colours and designs of a woman's dress indicated her region and her marital and economic status, while most motifs had names rather than fixed meanings. A bride's thobe is often made by hand by women in the family, with work beginning months or years ahead. Read the full guide to Palestinian wedding traditions.

pinterest.title: Palestinian Dabke at a Wedding: How to Plan the Dance Floor
pinterest.description: In 2023, UNESCO inscribed dabkeh, traditional dance in Palestine, on its Representative List. Dancers stand in a straight line or a semicircle, clasping hands and shoulders, jumping and striking the ground with their feet. So plan a long, solid dance floor, live music and a venue sound limit that suits drums and wind instruments. More Palestinian wedding traditions in our guide.

slides: A Palestinian wedding is rarely one evening. Here is the sequence, in order.
1. Tulbeh: the formal asking. The groom's family, led by an elder, visits the bride's family to ask for her hand. Tea, coffee and traditional sweets are served.
2. Sahra: an evening party for friends and family that runs into the early morning. The groom may be shaved in front of the guests while everyone cheers and sings.
3. Laylat al-henna: a gathering for the bride and her closest women. The paste is prepared on a tray decorated with flowers, and the women sing songs of joy and love.
4. Tatreez: Palestinian embroidery, inscribed by UNESCO in 2021. The bride's thobe is where it reaches its height, often made by hand by women in the family.
5. Zaffeh: the wedding procession, with its own music. What every zaffeh needs is a route through the venue.
6. Dabke: inscribed by UNESCO in 2023. A line of dancers, hands and shoulders clasped, stamping in time. Plan a long, solid dance floor.
Bringing these customs to your wedding? Tell a Wedded Advisor how your families celebrate, and we will help shape the evenings into one plan.
instagram_carousel.caption:
A Palestinian wedding is rarely one evening. It is a sequence: a family visit to ask, nights of singing, a henna gathering, a march with drums, a line of dancers stamping in time.

Our new guide follows the order of a real celebration, from the tulbeh to the zaffeh and dabke, and traces each meaning to UNESCO, museum dress collections and published reference works. Where a story is only "often told", we say so.

Palestinian families include Muslim and Christian households, and there is no single correct version, only the version your families recognise.

Planning to carry these customs into a wedding at home in Australia or abroad? The guide covers what each one asks of a venue: a separate henna night space, a route for the zaffeh, a long dance floor for dabke and room in the run sheet for guest-led singing.

Read the full guide via the link in our bio, or send us a message to speak with a Wedded Advisor about how your families celebrate.
